name: Pramiracetam
lead: Pramiracetam is a synthetic nootropic of the racetam family, derived from piracetam and taken by mouth. People who use it for self-improvement are mainly after sharper focus, memory and mental stamina, which feed into study, work and training consistency and, through those, the habits that go into a better physique and appearance [4][2].

It was developed by Parke-Davis in the late 1970s and has been marketed as a prescription medicine in a few European countries, for example as Pramistar, for memory and attention problems in older adults. It has not been approved by the US FDA for any indication [13].

Published research includes a small randomized placebo-controlled trial in young men with memory problems after head injury or oxygen deprivation, pharmacokinetic work in healthy volunteers, a small Alzheimer's study, and a body of animal studies [7][5][6][10].

chain: Claimed support for focus, memory and mental energy
More consistent studying, training and routines
angle.text: Users take pramiracetam as a cognition aid, hoping for better concentration and recall during demanding days. Any link to appearance runs through that indirect chain of focus and consistency rather than a direct effect on the body.

infobox: Not FDA-approved; prescription medicine in some European countries [13]

paras: In medicine, pramiracetam has been used and studied for memory and attention problems in older adults and for cognitive deficits after traumatic brain injury [4][7]. In Italy it was sold by Menarini as Pramistar until the marketing authorization was withdrawn at the manufacturer's request in 2020; it remains listed in Latvia [13].
Healthy adults also take it as a nootropic for memory and focus. Controlled studies in unimpaired people are scarce [13].

Scientists at Parke-Davis, a division of Warner-Lambert, discovered pramiracetam in the late 1970s, and its patents expired in 1996.[14] Warner-Lambert dropped an Alzheimer's indication after mixed phase II results and then explored it as an add-on to electroconvulsive therapy for major depression, partly to use orphan-drug exclusivity.[14]

In 1991 Menarini received European rights and continued developing it for dementias, while Cambridge Neuroscience received US and other rights; the company's US orphan designation for the ECT use was withdrawn when it abandoned the drug.[14] Menarini sells it as Pramistar, mainly in Italy and some Eastern European countries; two Italian brands, Remen and Neupramir, had their authorisations revoked.[14] Small trials mentioned on Wikipedia include one in four people with cognitive problems after head injury, two small Ukrainian trials in cerebrovascular disease and concussion, and an Italian study in healthy people with scopolamine-induced amnesia.[14]

Pramiracetam is Schedule 4, prescription-only, in Australia and is not FDA-approved in the United States.[14] It is sold as a prescription medicine in a few European markets, and Italy's authorisation was withdrawn at the manufacturer's request in 2020.[13]

Pramiracetam is taken by people seeking focus and memory support for study and work, which carries over into training consistency and daily routine.[4][2] It is a structural relative of piracetam, and reviews describe the racetams as sharing a profile of low reported toxicity with mechanisms that are not fully settled.[2][3]

A pharmacokinetic trial gave single oral doses to healthy male volunteers in a double-blind randomized design; peak levels came 2 to 3 hours after dosing, half-life was 4.5 to 6.5 hours, and no significant side effects were observed at any dose [5].

A double-blind placebo-controlled trial in young males with memory problems after head injury or anoxia reported clinically significant improvement in memory measures, especially delayed recall, compared with placebo [7].

A small two-phase trial in 10 patients with probable Alzheimer's disease found that eight showed a best dose in the first phase, but only two improved to a similar degree on replication [6]. A trial in healthy volunteers examined effects on scopolamine-induced amnesia [8]. Reviews describe pramiracetam as reportedly improving cognitive deficits linked to traumatic brain injury [4].
Beyond these small trials, there is no large published trial in healthy people, and the earlier phase II work for Alzheimer's did not lead to approval.[14][6]

The mechanism is not settled. Reviews of piracetam-type nootropics describe an interaction with cholinergic systems, and note that parallel experiments with different racetams sometimes give divergent results [1][3]. Pramiracetam increased high-affinity choline uptake in rat hippocampal tissue [11], inhibited the enzyme prolyl endopeptidase in vitro [9], and, as with other racetams, its memory effects in animals depended on adrenal steroids [3][12]. Animal dose-response curves are inverted-U shaped [6].
In volunteers, peak concentrations and exposure rose linearly with dose, and clearance and half-life were independent of dose [5].

Reviews describe racetams as having very low toxicity and lacking serious side effects [2]. No significant side effects were seen in the volunteer pharmacokinetic trial up to 1,600 mg single doses [5]. Headache, nausea, dizziness, insomnia and stomach upset have been reported as mild effects [13].

claims.believers: Users of nootropic stacks describe it as a racetam for concentration and recall.[4]
claims.experts: A double-blind trial in young men with head injury or oxygen deprivation reported better delayed recall than placebo, and no trial in healthy people has compared it with piracetam.[7]

card.summary: A racetam nootropic taken orally for focus and memory, which people use to support study, work and consistent training.
card.note: Not FDA-approved; prescription medicine in a few European countries.

quick.overview:
Pramiracetam is a racetam, a relative of piracetam, taken by mouth to support memory and concentration. It has been sold as a medicine in some European countries for memory and attention problems in older adults.

People interested in looks use it indirectly: better focus can mean steadier study, work and training routines.
quick.mechanism: How it works is not settled. Research points to cholinergic effects and interactions with adrenal steroids, and animal studies show an inverted-U dose response.
quick.risks: Reviews describe racetams as very low in toxicity, and a volunteer trial saw no significant side effects. Mild headache, nausea or insomnia are reported. It is not FDA-approved.
